was.title: WAS (Web Application Server)
was.content:
A WAS is the server that runs the main business logic of a web application.
A Spring Boot backend server can be considered a WAS.
Role of WAS
A WAS receives requests from clients, processes the logic, communicates with the database, and returns responses.

Client → WAS → DB
Client ← WAS ← DB

In a chat system, a WAS can handle:

creating chat rooms
saving messages
retrieving chat history
managing WebSocket connections
publishing messages to Redis
handling read/unread status
sending notifications

Web Server vs WAS
A Web Server mainly handles static files, such as:

HTML
CSS
JavaScript
images

A WAS handles dynamic application logic, such as:

login
order lookup
chat message storage
database queries
notifications

Web Server → static files
WAS → business logic
Why Use Multiple WAS Servers?
If there are many users, one WAS may not be enough to handle all requests.
So multiple WAS servers are used to divide the traffic.
Load Balancer
   ↓
WAS 1
WAS 2
WAS 3
This improves performance, availability, and scalability.
Related: Load Balancing WebSocket

cia-triad.title: CIA Triad
cia-triad.content:
The CIA Triad is a basic cybersecurity model used to protect information.
CIA stands for:
Confidentiality

Only authorized people can access the information.

Example: using passwords, encryption, and access control to protect private data.
Integrity

Information should be accurate and not changed without permission.

Example: preventing someone from modifying a file or database record.
Availability

Systems and data should be accessible when needed.

Example: keeping a website online and preventing downtime from attacks or failures.

computer-network.title: Computer Network
computer-network.content:
A computer network is a group of connected devices that can communicate and share data with each other.
Examples of devices include computers, phones, servers, routers, and printers.
Main Purpose
Computer networks allow devices to:

share data
access the internet
communicate with servers
use shared resources like printers or files

Common Types

LAN

A local network in a small area, such as a home, school, or office.


WAN

A large network that connects devices across cities, countries, or the world.


Internet

The largest global network connecting millions of devices.



Important Components

Router

Sends data between different networks.


Switch

Connects devices within the same local network.


Server

Provides services or data to other devices.


Client

A device that requests data or services from a server.



Simple Example
When you open a website, your computer sends a request through the network to a web server.
The server sends the website data back to your computer.

cryptography.title: Cryptography
cryptography.content:
Cryptography is the practice of protecting information by converting it into a secure form.
It is used to keep data private, verify identities, and protect data from being changed.
Main Purposes

Confidentiality

Keeps information secret from unauthorized people.


Integrity

Makes sure data has not been changed.


Authentication

Verifies the identity of users, systems, or websites.


Non-repudiation

Prevents someone from denying that they performed an action.



Common Concepts

Encryption

Converts readable data into unreadable data.


Decryption

Converts encrypted data back into readable data.


Key

A secret value used to encrypt or decrypt data.


Hashing

Creates a fixed-size value from data to check integrity.



Simple Example
When a website uses HTTPS, cryptography helps protect passwords and personal information while they travel between the browser and the server.

cybersecurity.title: Cybersecurity
cybersecurity.content:
Cybersecurity is about understanding how systems break, how people make mistakes, and how to protect information from threats.
I became interested in cybersecurity through internship, and studying security fundamentals.
Related: CompTIA Security+

defense-in-depth.title: Defense in Depth
defense-in-depth.content:
Defense in Depth is a cybersecurity strategy that uses multiple layers of protection.
The idea is that if one security layer fails, other layers can still protect the system.
Examples of Security Layers

Firewall

Blocks suspicious network traffic.


Access Control

Limits who can access systems and data.


MFA

Adds extra verification during login.


Encryption

Protects data even if it is stolen.


Monitoring

Detects suspicious activity.


Backups

Helps recover data after an incident.



Simple Example
A company may use a firewall, strong passwords, MFA, antivirus software, and backups together.
Even if an attacker bypasses one layer, they still have to get through the others.

jwt.title: JWT (JSON Web Token)
jwt.content:
JWT (JSON Web Token)
One-line summary
JWT is a signed token that proves who the user is.
The client sends it with every API request, and the server verifies it before allowing access.
Login successful
→ Server issues JWT
→ Client stores JWT
→ Client sends JWT in Authorization header
→ Server verifies JWT
→ Request is allowed or rejected

Why JWT is used
In older session-based login, the server stores login state.
User logs in
→ Server creates session
→ Browser keeps session cookie
→ Server checks session on each request
With JWT, the server usually does not store the session.
User logs in
→ Server creates JWT
→ Client stores token
→ Client sends token with each request
→ Server verifies token every time
This is useful for a multi-server setup.
WAS 1
WAS 2
Redis
DB
If users can hit different WAS servers, JWT is convenient because each server can verify the token without relying on one server’s session memory.

JWT structure
A JWT has 3 parts:
Header.Payload.Signature
Example shape:
xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz
1. Header
Contains token type and signing algorithm.
{
  "alg": "HS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}
2. Payload
Contains claims, which are pieces of information about the user or token.
Example:
{
  "userId": "admin01",
  "role": "ADMIN",
  "orgCd": "DIVE",
  "exp": 1720000000
}
Common claims:





























ClaimMeaningsubSubject, often user IDroleUser role or authorityorgCdOrganization/company codeiatIssued at timeexpExpiration time
3. Signature
Used to check whether the token was changed or forged.
The server signs the token using a secret key or private key.
If someone changes the payload, the signature check fails.

Important security point
JWT payload is not automatically encrypted.
It is usually Base64URL-encoded, which means people can decode and read the payload.
So do not put sensitive data inside JWT.
Avoid putting:
password
resident registration number
credit card number
private personal information
Okay to put:
userId
role
orgCd
token expiration time

Related: Spring Security Backend

make notes about REST API, Spring Security, Spring Boot(controler, service, mapper), MyBatis, PostgreSQL, JDBC,
JWT

kcl.title: KCL
kcl.content:
Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL)
KCL: The total current entering a node equals the total current leaving the node.
In other words, charge does not disappear or build up at a node.
\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}
or
\sum I = 0
where currents entering can be positive and currents leaving can be negative.
Example
If 3 currents meet at one node:
I_1 = I_2 + I_3
This means the current coming into the node splits into two paths.
When to use KCL
Use KCL when analyzing nodes in a circuit.
KCL is the basis of nodal analysis.

Quick Comparison




















LawMain IdeaUsed ForKCLCurrents at a node sum to zeroNode analysisKVLVoltages around a loop sum to zeroLoop/mesh analysis
Related

Circuit Analysis
Ohm’s Law
Nodal Analysis
Mesh Analysis

kvl.title: KVL
kvl.content:
Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL)
KVL: The sum of all voltage rises and drops around a closed loop is zero.
Energy is conserved around a loop.
\sum V = 0
Example
For a simple loop with one voltage source and two resistors:
V_s - V_1 - V_2 = 0
so
V_s = V_1 + V_2
This means the source voltage is divided across the resistors.
When to use KVL
Use KVL when analyzing loops in a circuit.
KVL is the basis of mesh analysis.

Intuition

KVL: voltage gained and lost around a loop balances out.
KCL: what comes into a node must go out.

load-balancing.title: Load Balancing
load-balancing.content:
Load balancing means distributing traffic across multiple servers.
When many users access a service, one server may become overloaded.
A load balancer solves this by sending requests to different WAS servers.
Client
  ↓
Load Balancer
  ↓
WAS 1 / WAS 2 / WAS 3
Role of a Load Balancer
A load balancer receives client requests and forwards them to an available server.
Example:

User A → WAS 1
User B → WAS 2
User C → WAS 3

Why Load Balancing Is Used
Load balancing is used to:

prevent one server from being overloaded
improve system performance
keep the service running even if one server fails
make the system easier to scale

Common Load Balancing Methods
Round Robin
Requests are distributed to servers in order.

1st request → WAS 1
2nd request → WAS 2
3rd request → WAS 3
4th request → WAS 1

Least Connections
The request goes to the server with the fewest active connections.

Choose the WAS with the least number of connections

IP Hash
The same user is usually sent to the same server based on their IP address.

Same user → same WAS

Load Balancing with WebSocket
WebSocket connections stay open after they are created.
Because of this, WebSocket systems need to handle load balancing carefully.
For example:

User A → WAS 1
User B → WAS 2

If User A sends a message, only WAS 1 receives it at first.
To deliver the message to User B on WAS 2, the servers need to share messages.
This is where Redis Pub/Sub can be used.
Related: Redis WebSocket WAS

mosfet.title: MOSFET
mosfet.content:
MOSFET: Metal-Oxide-Semicondcutor Field-Effect Transistor
A MOSFET is a transistor that controls current using voltage.
1. MOSFET Terminals
A MOSFET is usually drawn as a 3-terminal device, but physically it has 4 terminals:

Gate
Source
Drain
Body

For many MOSFETs, the source and drain are physically symmetric.
However, in circuit operation, we call one side “source” and the other side “drain” depending on the applied voltages and current direction.
2. NMOS and PMOS Body Connection
NMOS
An NMOS transistor is usually built in a p-type body.
This p-type body can be:

p-substrate
p-well

For NMOS, the body is usually connected to the lowest voltage, normally ground (GND).
This helps keep the body-source junction reverse-biased.
PMOS
A PMOS transistor is usually built in an n-well.
For PMOS, the body is usually connected to the highest voltage, normally VDD.
This also helps keep the body-source junction reverse-biased.
3. MOSFET Operation Regions
A MOSFET has three main operation regions:

Cut-off
Triode / Linear
Saturation

4. Cut-off Region
In cut-off, the MOSFET is mostly off.
For NMOS:
[
V_{GS} < V_{TH}
]
The gate-to-source voltage is not large enough to strongly turn on the channel, so ideally no drain current flows.
In real devices, a very small leakage current can still flow.
5. Triode / Linear Region
In triode region, the MOSFET is on, but it behaves more like a voltage-controlled resistor.
For NMOS:
[
V_{GS} > V_{TH}
]
and
[
V_{DS} < V_{GS} - V_{TH}
]
In this region, the MOSFET has an on-resistance called:
[
R_{on}
]
This region is often used when the MOSFET acts like a switch or resistor.
6. Saturation Region
In saturation region, the MOSFET behaves more like a current source.
For NMOS:
[
V_{GS} > V_{TH}
]
and
[
V_{DS} > V_{GS} - V_{TH}
]
Ideally, once the MOSFET enters saturation, the drain current becomes almost constant even if (V_{DS}) increases.
This is very important in analog circuits because amplifiers need a stable operating current.
7. Why Saturation Matters in Analog Circuits
In analog design, we often want MOSFETs to operate in the saturation region.
The reason is that in saturation, the drain current is mainly controlled by (V_{GS}), not (V_{DS}).
So even if (V_{DS}) changes, the current stays relatively stable.
This makes it possible to define a stable DC operating point, and then analyze small AC signal changes around that point.
In simple terms:

DC analysis decides where the transistor sits.
AC analysis studies how the circuit responds to small changes around that point.

8. Three Important MOSFET Effects
Real MOSFETs are not ideal.
There are three important non-ideal effects:

Channel Length Modulation, CLM
Body Effect
Parasitic Capacitance

9. Channel Length Modulation, CLM
Ideally, in saturation, drain current should stay constant as (V_{DS}) increases.
But in real MOSFETs, the drain current slightly increases as (V_{DS}) increases.
This effect is called channel length modulation.
It becomes stronger when the channel length is shorter.
So from the CLM point of view, using a longer channel length can make the current source more ideal.
In equations, CLM is often modeled using (\lambda):
[
I_D = I_{D,sat}(1 + \lambda V_{DS})
]
The parameter (\lambda) represents how much the current increases with (V_{DS}).
10. Body Effect
The body effect happens when the body voltage is different from the source voltage.
For NMOS, the body is usually connected to ground.
If the source is also at ground, then:
[
V_{SB} = 0
]
So there is no body effect.
But if the source voltage is not equal to the body voltage, then:
[
V_{SB} \neq 0
]
The threshold voltage (V_{TH}) changes.
In simple terms:

Body effect means the body-source voltage changes the threshold voltage.

11. Parasitic Capacitance
Parasitic capacitance is unwanted capacitance that naturally appears inside the MOSFET.
Whenever two conductive regions are separated by an insulating material, capacitance can form.
In MOSFETs, parasitic capacitances can appear between terminals such as:

Gate–Source
Gate–Drain
Drain–Body
Source–Body

These capacitances are usually unwanted because they affect speed, delay, and coupling.
Parasitic capacitance is strongly affected by the transistor width.
Larger width usually creates larger parasitic capacitance.
12. DC Analysis
DC analysis finds the DC operating point of the circuit.
For example, in a common-source amplifier, if (V_{in}) is below (V_{TH}), the NMOS is off and almost no current flows.
Then:
[
V_{out} \approx V_{DD}
]
As (V_{in}) increases above (V_{TH}), the NMOS turns on, current flows through the resistor, and (V_{out}) starts to decrease.
To build an amplifier, we usually choose (V_{in}), (R_D), and the MOSFET size so that the transistor operates in saturation.
A key goal in analog design is:

Bias the transistors so they operate in the correct region, usually saturation.

13. AC Analysis
After the DC operating point is set, AC analysis studies how small input changes are amplified.
The MOSFET can be replaced by a small-signal model.
Important small-signal parameters include:
Transconductance
[
g_m
]
This tells how much the drain current changes when (V_{GS}) changes.
In simple terms:

(g_m) tells how strongly the MOSFET converts voltage change into current change.

Output Resistance
[
r_o
]
This comes from channel length modulation.
If CLM is small, (r_o) is large, and the MOSFET behaves more like an ideal current source.
Body Transconductance
[
g_{mb}
]
This comes from body effect.
It models how changes in (V_{BS}) affect the drain current.
Summary
A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled current device.
In digital circuits, it is often used as a switch.
In analog circuits, it is biased at a proper DC operating point and used as a controlled current source.
The most important analog idea is:

Set the MOSFET in saturation for DC bias, then use small-signal analysis to understand AC amplification.

redis.title: Redis
redis.content:
Redis is an in-memory data store.
It stores data in memory, so it is much faster than a traditional disk-based database.
Redis is commonly used for:

caching
session storage
real-time ranking
message brokering
Pub/Sub messaging

Key Idea
Redis stores data in a key-value format.

key → value

Example:

user:1 → Melania
chatRoom:100 → active

Redis Pub/Sub
Redis Pub/Sub is a real-time messaging feature.
Pub/Sub stands for:

Publisher: sends a message
Channel: the path where the message is sent
Subscriber: receives messages from a channel

Publisher → Redis Channel → Subscribers
Why Redis Pub/Sub Is Used in Chat
In a chat system, users may be connected to different WAS servers.

User A → WAS 1
User B → WAS 2

If User A sends a message, WAS 1 receives it first.
However, User B is connected to WAS 2, not WAS 1.
So WAS 1 publishes the message to Redis.
Then all WAS servers subscribed to that Redis channel receive the message.
User A → WAS 1 → Redis Pub/Sub → WAS 2 → User B
This allows users to receive messages no matter which WAS server they are connected to.
Important Point
Redis Pub/Sub does not permanently store messages.
It only delivers messages to subscribers that are currently connected.
Therefore, chat messages should still be saved in a database.

DB → stores chat history
Redis Pub/Sub → delivers real-time messages between servers

Related: WebSocket WAS

risk-management.title: Risk Management
risk-management.content:
Risk Management is the process of identifying, assessing, and reducing risks that could harm an organization.
In cybersecurity, risk usually means the chance that a threat will exploit a vulnerability and cause damage.
Main Steps

Identify Risks


Find possible threats, vulnerabilities, and assets that need protection.


Assess Risks


Understand how likely the risk is and how serious the impact would be.


Prioritize Risks


Focus on the risks that could cause the most damage.


Treat Risks


Decide how to handle the risk.

Risk Treatment Options

Avoid

Stop doing the risky activity.


Reduce

Add security controls to lower the risk.


Transfer

Share the risk with another party, such as insurance.


Accept

Accept the risk if it is low or unavoidable.



Simple Example
If a company stores customer data, there is a risk of data leakage.
The company can reduce this risk by using encryption, access control, and regular security monitoring.

social-engineering.title: Social Engineering
social-engineering.content:
Social Engineering is a cyberattack method that tricks people instead of attacking systems directly.
Attackers use human emotions like trust, fear, urgency, or curiosity to make people reveal sensitive information or take unsafe actions.
Common Examples

Phishing

Fake emails or messages that try to steal passwords or personal information.


Impersonation

Pretending to be someone trusted, like a coworker, manager, or IT support.


Pretexting

Creating a fake story to convince someone to share information.

ssl-and-tls.title: SSL/TLS
ssl-and-tls.content:
SSL/TLS is a security protocol used to protect data sent over the internet.
It is commonly used in HTTPS to secure communication between a browser and a web server.
SSL vs TLS

SSL stands for Secure Sockets Layer.
TLS stands for Transport Layer Security. TLS is the newer and more secure version of SSL.

Main Purposes

Encryption

Prevents others from reading the data.


Authentication

Verifies that the server is really who it claims to be.


Integrity

Ensures the data was not changed during transmission.



Simple Example
When a website uses https://, TLS helps protect sensitive data like passwords, payment information, and personal details.
Key Idea
SSL/TLS makes internet communication secure by encrypting data and verifying identities.

thread-scheduling.title: Thread Scheduling
thread-scheduling.content:
What is Thread Scheduling?
Thread scheduling is the process of deciding the order in which threads use the CPU.
Since multiple threads may be ready to run at the same time, the operating system needs a scheduling policy to decide which thread gets CPU time first, how long it runs, and when another thread should run.

Types of Thread Scheduling
1. Preemptive Scheduling
Preemptive scheduling is a scheduling method where the operating system can forcibly stop the currently running thread and assign the CPU to another thread.
In this method, a thread does not necessarily run until it finishes. Instead, the operating system may interrupt it depending on the scheduling policy.
Examples of preemptive scheduling policies include:

Round Robin
Priority-Based Scheduling
Shortest Job First

Advantages
Preemptive scheduling allows the CPU to be shared more dynamically among multiple threads. This can improve responsiveness and make the system feel faster, especially when many threads are running.
Disadvantages
Because threads may be switched frequently, context switching costs occur. A context switch takes time because the system must save the current thread’s state and load another thread’s state.

2. Non-Preemptive Scheduling
Non-preemptive scheduling is a scheduling method where once a thread gets the CPU, it continues using the CPU until it finishes or voluntarily gives up control.
In this method, the operating system does not forcibly interrupt the running thread.
Advantages
Non-preemptive scheduling is simpler to implement and does not cause frequent context switching costs.
Disadvantages
It may be difficult to use the CPU efficiently when multiple threads are waiting. If one thread runs for a long time, other threads may have to wait for a long time before they can execute.

Thread States
1. New / Ready State
This is the state where a thread has been created and allocated in memory. The thread is ready to use the CPU, but it has not been assigned CPU time yet.
2. Running State
This is the state where a thread is currently using the CPU.
3. Not Runnable State
This is the state where a thread exists in memory but cannot currently use the CPU.
4. Dead / Terminated State
This is the state where a thread has finished its execution and is no longer active.
Related: Thread

thread.title: Thread
thread.content:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution inside a process.
A process can contain multiple threads, and each thread can run a different task. Threads in the same process share memory, which makes communication faster but also requires careful synchronization.
A thread allows a program to do multiple tasks at the same time.
Process vs Thread
A process is the whole running program.
A thread is a worker inside that process.
Process
 ├── Thread 1
 ├── Thread 2
 └── Thread 3

vulnerability-management.title: Vulnerability Management
vulnerability-management.content:
Vulnerability Management is the process of finding, assessing, prioritizing, and fixing security weaknesses in systems, applications, and networks.
The goal is to reduce the chance that attackers can exploit known vulnerabilities.
Main Steps

Identify


Scan systems to find vulnerabilities.


Assess


Understand how serious each vulnerability is.


Prioritize


Fix the most critical risks first.


Remediate


Patch, configure, or remove the vulnerable component.


Monitor


Continuously check for new vulnerabilities.

Key Idea
Not every vulnerability has the same risk.
Vulnerability management focuses on fixing the vulnerabilities that are most likely to cause real damage.
Simple Example
If a server has outdated software with a known security flaw, the team should patch it before attackers can exploit it.

websocket.title: WebSocket
websocket.content:
WebSocket is a technology that allows real-time two-way communication between a client and a server.
Unlike normal HTTP, WebSocket keeps the connection open.
This allows both the client and the server to send messages at any time.
HTTP vs WebSocket
HTTP is request-response based.

Client → Request → Server
Client ← Response ← Server

The server usually responds only when the client sends a request.
WebSocket keeps a continuous connection.

Client ↔ Server

The server can send messages to the client without waiting for a new request.
Why WebSocket Is Used
WebSocket is useful for real-time features, such as:

chat
live notifications
live location sharing
real-time dashboards

In a chat system, users should receive new messages immediately without refreshing the page.

User A → Server → User B

WebSocket Flow

The client requests a WebSocket connection.
The server accepts the connection.
The connection stays open.
The client and server exchange messages in real time.
The connection closes when the user leaves or the network disconnects.

Connect → Keep Connection → Send/Receive Messages → Disconnect
WebSocket in a Chat System
In a simple chat system:
User A → WebSocket → WAS → WebSocket → User B
However, in a multi-server system, users may be connected to different WAS servers.

User A → WAS 1
User B → WAS 2

In that case, Redis Pub/Sub helps deliver messages between servers.
User A
→ WAS 1
→ Redis Pub/Sub
→ WAS 2
→ User B
Related: Redis

zero-trust.title: Zero Trust Model
zero-trust.content:
Zero Trust Model is a cybersecurity model based on the idea of “Never trust, always verify.”
In traditional security, users inside the company network were often trusted. However, Zero Trust does not automatically trust anyone, even if they are inside the network.
The main principles are:

Never Trust, Always Verify

Every user and device must be verified before access is allowed.


Least Privilege Access

Users only get the minimum access they need.


Continuous Monitoring

User activity is constantly checked, even after login.



For example, even if an employee logs into a company system, Zero Trust may still check their password, MFA, device status, location, and access permissions.
In short, Zero Trust means every access request must be verified instead of automatically trusted.

semiconductor/ic.title: IC (Integrated Circuit)
semiconductor/ic.content:
An integrated circuit, or IC, is a small electronic circuit built on a single piece of semiconductor material, usually silicon.
IC, Chip, and Semiconductor

Semiconductor

A material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled. Silicon is the most commonly used semiconductor material.


Integrated Circuit

An electronic circuit containing many components fabricated on a semiconductor material.


Chip

A common informal term for an integrated circuit or the small piece of silicon containing it.



Memory and Processing ICs
These ICs store data or process information.

NAND Flash
SoC
LPDDR
MCU

Power Management ICs
These ICs control voltage, current, charging, and power distribution.

Voltage Regulator
Charging IC
PMIC
Wireless Charging IC

Connectivity and Interface ICs
These ICs allow electronic devices to communicate with other devices or components.

Bluetooth IC
Wi-Fi Module
NFC Controller
UWB SoC
USB-C Controller

Sensor ICs
These ICs detect changes in the physical environment.

Temperature Sensor IC
Accelerometer and Gyroscope

Audio and Input ICs
These ICs process audio signals or user input.

Audio Amplifier
Digitizer

RF ICs and Modules
These components generate, amplify, transmit, or receive radio-frequency signals.

RF Transmitter
RF Front-End Module
Power Amplifier

Key Idea
Each semiconductor IC is designed for a specific function.
In an electronic device, multiple ICs work together. For example, a smartphone may use:

an SoC for processing
LPDDR for temporary memory
NAND Flash for storage
a PMIC for power management
Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, NFC, and UWB ICs for wireless communication
sensor ICs for motion and temperature detection
an audio amplifier for speaker output

semiconductor/index.title: Semiconductor
semiconductor/index.content:
A semiconductor is a material that can act as both a conductor and an insulator depending on conditions.
It is the foundation of modern electronics because it can control the flow of electric current.
Common Materials

Silicon

The most commonly used semiconductor material.


Germanium

Used in some specialized electronic devices.



Key Idea
Semiconductors are useful because their electrical behavior can be controlled.
This makes them important for building electronic components such as:

Diode
Transistor
IC
computer chips
sensors
memory devices

Doping
Doping means adding small amounts of impurities to a semiconductor to change its electrical properties.
There are two main types:

N-type semiconductor

Has extra electrons.


P-type semiconductor

Has extra holes.



Simple Example
A transistor uses semiconductor material to control current flow.
This allows computers and phones to process information.
